title: Effects on Microstructure and Microhardness of MgO (24%)-Stabilized Zirconia Coatings Produced by Atmospheric Plasma-Spraying and Laser Cladding
content: The selection of ceramic materials and coating methods should focus on achieving an optimal microstructure and hardness for applications that require high-temperature resistance. The development of zirconia coatings with enhanced mechanical properties through processing techniques is an intriguing area for ceramic coating applications. Microhardness serves as a key indicator of mechanical properties for assessing the ability of materials to resist deformation. It is significantly influenced by the existing variety of inherent microstructural defects in the coatings. A deeper understanding of the microstructural mechanisms and their associated mechanical properties will enhance hardness, wear resistance, and contribute to extending the lifetime of thermal barrier coatings (TBCs). The durability of coatings strongly depends on their mechanical properties and the adhesion strength of the deposited layers. Techniques such as atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) and laser cladding are commonly used for depositing zirconia (ZrO2) coatings. In thermal spraying, such as APS, a high-temperature plasma jet is employed to melt and accelerate ZrO2 particles, which then bond to the substrate through impact and splat formation. Laser cladding relies on localized laser heating to melt ZrO2 and a thin layer of the substrate surface. Metal oxides such as CaO (5 wt.%), MgO (15-24 wt.%), or Y2O3 (6-12 wt.%) are added to ZrO2 to stabilize the tetragonal and/or cubic phases at the ambient temperatures [1,2]. MgO (24%)-stabilized ZrO2 is more cost-effective expensive and is typically used in low-temperature applications, such as jet engines exhaust nozzle [3]. This study investigate the cross-sectional microstructures and microhardness of the MgO (24%)-stabilized ZrO2 coatings produced by both APS and laser cladding techniqes.
